rewritten_text: "They ought to concern you, Dorian. Every gentleman cares about his reputation. You cannot want people speaking of you as something corrupt and contemptible. Of course, you have social standing, money, and all the rest, but those things aren't everything. Understand, I don't believe these rumours. At least, I cannot believe them when I look at you. Sin inscribes itself on a man's face; it cannot stay hidden. People sometimes speak of secret vices, but there is no such thing. A man's depravity appears in the lines around his mouth, the sag of his eyelids, even the shape of his hands. Someone—you know him, although I won't name him—asked me to paint his portrait last year. I had never met him or heard anything about him then, though I've heard plenty since. He offered a ridiculous amount of money, but I turned him down. Something about the shape of his fingers disgusted me. Now I know my impression was completely justified. His life is appalling. But you, Dorian, with that clear, radiant, innocent face and your extraordinary, untroubled youth—I cannot believe anything bad about you. Yet I hardly ever see you, and you no longer visit the studio. When you aren't with me and I hear the dreadful things people whisper, I don't know how to answer. Why does someone like the Duke of Berwick leave a club room the moment you enter? Why do so many gentlemen in London refuse both to visit your house and to invite you into theirs? Lord Staveley used to be your friend. I saw him at dinner last week. Your name came up because of the miniatures you've lent to the exhibition at the Dudley. Staveley curled his lip and said that, whatever your exquisite artistic taste, no innocent girl should be allowed to know you, and no virtuous woman should sit in the same room with you. I reminded him that you were my friend and asked what he meant. He told me, plainly, in front of everyone. It was horrible! Why does your friendship prove so disastrous to young men? There was that unfortunate boy in the Guards who killed himself. You were a close friend of his. Then there was Sir Henry Ashton, who had to leave England with his reputation ruined.

Mrs. Otis also tells me that these jewels are worth a great deal of money and would sell for a very high price. I should add that she knows a good deal about Art, having enjoyed several winters in Boston as a girl. Given all this, Lord Canterville, I am sure you understand why I cannot allow anyone in my family to keep them. Such vain ornaments and trinkets may suit, or even be necessary to, the dignity of the British aristocracy. But they would be entirely out of place among people raised on the strict and, I believe, everlasting principles of republican simplicity. I should perhaps mention that Virginia very much hopes you will let her keep the box as a reminder of your unfortunate but misguided ancestor. It is extremely old and therefore rather damaged, so perhaps you will consider granting her wish. I admit I am surprised that any child of mine should sympathize with anything medieval. I can explain it only by remembering that Virginia was born in one of your London suburbs shortly after Mrs. Otis returned from visiting Athens.'

Lord Canterville listened to the worthy Minister with a very serious expression, occasionally tugging his grey moustache to hide a smile. When Mr. Otis finished, he warmly shook his hand. 'My dear sir, your lovely daughter did my unfortunate ancestor, Sir Simon, an enormous kindness. My family and I owe her a great deal for her remarkable courage and determination. The jewels plainly belong to her. Indeed, if I were cruel enough to take them away, I believe that wicked old fellow would rise from his grave within a fortnight and make my life a misery. As for calling them heirlooms, nothing counts as an heirloom unless a will or legal document identifies it as one, and nobody even knew these jewels existed. I assure you, I have no greater claim to them than your butler. When Miss Virginia is older, I expect she will enjoy having lovely things to wear. Besides, Mr. Otis, you forget that you bought both the furniture and the ghost at their agreed value. Anything belonging to the ghost became yours immediately. However busy Sir Simon may have been in the corridor at night, he was legally dead, and you purchased his possessions.'

Perdita went unnamed, yet I could scarcely doubt that his love for her explained his wavering intentions. And who merited love more than my generous-minded sister? Who better deserved the hand of this self-appointed king than she whose gaze might have belonged to the sovereign of nations? She loved him as he loved her, though disappointment had subdued her passion, while ambition fiercely contested his.

That evening we went together to the House. Although Raymond knew the approaching debate would examine and determine his projects and prospects, he remained cheerful and unconcerned. Entering the coffee-room, we were deafened by a murmur like ten thousand swarming beehives. Politicians stood in clusters, brows troubled, voices either loud or low. The aristocratic faction, comprising England's wealthiest and most influential men, seemed calmer than the rest, since the question would be considered without their intervention. Beside the fire stood Ryland with his followers. Born in obscurity, Ryland possessed an enormous fortune inherited from his manufacturer father. As a young man he had witnessed the king's abdication and the merging of Lords and Commons into one house. He had welcomed these advances of popular power and devoted his life to strengthening and extending them. Since that time the great landowners' influence had increased. At first, therefore, Ryland had viewed Lord Raymond's manoeuvres without displeasure, as they drew numerous adherents away from his opponents. Now, however, matters had gone too far. The impoverished nobility welcomed the prospect of restored monarchy as the means of recovering their vanished authority and privileges. The nearly extinguished spirit of royalty stirred again in men's minds. Willing slaves, making subjects of themselves, they stood ready to bow their necks beneath the yoke. A few upright and independent spirits still survived as supports of the state; but the common ear had tired of the word republic, and many—the outcome would show whether most—longed for the glitter and spectacle of kingship. Ryland rose in opposition. He declared that this faction had grown only through his tolerance; the hour for indulgence was now over, and a single sweep of his arm would brush aside the cobwebs obscuring his countrymen's vision.

Raymond's arrival in the coffee-room brought an almost shouted welcome from his friends. They crowded about him, reckoned their strength, and explained why they expected this or that member, still publicly uncommitted, to join their ranks.
